expectedText:
PROMISSORY NOTE (LOAN BETWEEN INDIVIDUALS)
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

PARTIES AND PRINCIPAL
FOR VALUE RECEIVED, Jordan Lee ("Borrower") promises to pay to Pat Morgan ("Lender"), or Lender's order, the principal sum of $5,000. This is a personal loan between Borrower and Lender, not a loan from a bank, credit union, or other licensed lending institution. This Note is unsecured: Borrower is not giving Lender a deed of trust, mortgage, security interest, or other lien on any property as security for repayment, and Lender's only recourse for nonpayment is a personal claim against Borrower, not a claim against any specific collateral. This Note is signed in Sacramento, California on November 28, 2026.

INTEREST-RATE LIMIT ON THIS LOAN
The California Constitution fixes the interest rate the parties to a loan like this one may set by written contract. If the loan or forbearance of money is used primarily for Jordan Lee's personal, family, or household purposes — a category that excludes money used primarily to buy, build, or improve real property, even though that can feel like a personal purpose — Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee may contract in writing for interest of up to 10 percent per year. If the loan is instead used for any other purpose, such as a business purpose, the ceiling is instead the higher of 10 percent per year or 5 percent per year plus a benchmark rate the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco sets for advances to member banks, measured as of a date tied to when the loan contract is made. This ceiling applies to a loan between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee because neither of them is acting in a category the Constitution exempts from these limits (for example, as a bank, credit union, or licensed pawnbroker), and — as described in the next clause — the fact that the loan is unsecured means the real-estate-broker exemption does not apply either. Which of the two percentage ceilings governs this particular loan therefore turns on whether its primary purpose is personal, family, or household, as described above, or something else.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]
  "For any loan or forbearance of any money, goods, or things in action, if the money, goods, or things in action are for use primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, at a rate not exceeding 10 percent per annum; provided, however, that any loan or forbearance of any money, goods or things in action the proceeds of which are used primarily for the purchase, construction or improvement of real property shall not be deemed to be a use primarily for personal, family or household purposes"
  — Cal. Const. art. XV, § 1, para. (1) (law.onecle.com text), California Constitution, 10%-per-year cap for a loan used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes (https://law.onecle.com/california/constitution/article-15.html)
  "For any loan or forbearance of any money, goods, or things in action for any use other than specified in paragraph (1), at a rate not exceeding the higher of (a) 10 percent per annum or (b) 5 percent per annum plus the rate prevailing on the 25th day of the month preceding the earlier of (i) the date of execution of the contract to make the loan or forbearance, or (ii) the date of making the loan or forbearance established by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco on advances to member banks under Sections 13 and 13a of the Federal Reserve Act as now in effect or hereafter from time to time amended"
  — Cal. Const. art. XV, § 1, para. (2) (law.onecle.com text), California Constitution, higher-of-10%-or-formula cap for a loan used for any other purpose (https://law.onecle.com/california/constitution/article-15.html)
  Known gap: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov returned a Cloudflare challenge page (and, through this tool's own fetcher, a direct 403) on repeated attempts to fetch Article XV, Section 1 directly, so the quotations below were read from law.onecle.com's text of the section instead, disclosed as sourceClass "mirror" rather than primary-official. Both quotations are two clauses of the same single constitutional sentence — paragraphs (1) and (2) of the same Section 1 — not two independent sources; they are quoted separately only because each states a different rate ceiling. This clause states the general, non-exempt rule and both rate tiers precisely as written, but it does not, and cannot, determine which tier actually governs a particular loan: that depends on the loan's primary purpose, a fact question this document does not resolve. For a loan that falls in the higher-of-10-percent-or-formula tier, this clause also does not state a current numeric value for the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco's member-bank advance rate, which is published periodically outside the constitutional text itself and would have to be looked up as of the relevant date to compute the actual ceiling. Separately, this research did not locate a current statute setting out a specific penalty (such as forfeiture or treble damages) for a loan that is made above the applicable ceiling; the pre-1979 statutory forfeiture penalty was tied to the prior version of this constitutional provision, and this document does not catalog what remedy, if any, currently follows from exceeding the limit described above.

WHY THE RELATED CIVIL CODE SECTIONS DO NOT CHANGE THIS LOAN'S RATE CEILING
A separate set of statutes, Civil Code sections 1916.1 through 1916.9, exists alongside the constitutional provision described in the Interest-Rate Limit clause above, but none of them sets a different interest-rate ceiling for a loan like the one between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee. Civil Code section 1916.1 exempts from the constitutional rate limits a loan that a person licensed in California as a real estate broker makes or arranges and that is secured, directly or collaterally, by a lien on real property — a description that does not fit this unsecured loan, since neither Pat Morgan nor Jordan Lee is acting as a licensed real estate broker and the loan carries no lien on real property. Civil Code section 1916.2 separately exempts loans made by an out-of-state public retirement or pension system, which likewise has nothing to do with a loan between two individuals. Civil Code sections 1916.5 through 1916.9 regulate how a variable interest rate may be structured, but only in a mortgage, deed of trust, real estate sales contract, or a note issued in connection with one of those, financing residential property of four units or fewer — rules this unsecured Note does not implicate, whether or not it bears a fixed interest rate.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]
  "The restrictions upon rates of interest contained in Section 1 of Article XV of the California Constitution shall not apply to any loan or forbearance made or arranged by any person licensed as a real estate broker by the State of California, and secured, directly or collaterally, in whole or in part by liens on real property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1916.1 (law.onecle.com text), California Civil Code, real-estate-broker exemption requires a loan secured by a lien on real property (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil/1916.1.html)
  "The restrictions upon rates of interest contained in Section 1 of Article XV of the California Constitution do not apply to any loans made by, or forbearances of, a public retirement or pension system that is created, authorized, and regulated by the laws of a state other than California, or the laws of a local agency of a state other than California."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1916.2 (law.onecle.com text), California Civil Code, out-of-state public pension system exemption (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil/1916.2.html)
  "This section shall be applicable only to a mortgage contract, deed of trust, real estate sales contract, or any note or negotiable instrument issued in connection therewith, when its purpose is to finance the purchase or construction of real property containing four or fewer residential units or on which four or fewer residential units are to be constructed."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1916.5(b)(1) (law.onecle.com text), California Civil Code, variable-interest-rate rules apply only to a mortgage, deed of trust, or real estate sales contract financing small residential property (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil/1916.5.html)

This clause is deliberately negative in scope: it explains why these particular statutes do not change the ceiling described in the Interest-Rate Limit clause for this unsecured, non-broker, non-pension, fixed- or simple-interest personal loan; it is not a complete inventory of every statute touching interest rates in California, and a loan with different features (for example, one secured by real property, or involving a pawnbroker, bank, or credit union) could bring a different provision of this same statutory group into play.

INTEREST
Interest accrues on the unpaid principal balance of this Note at the rate of 6% per year, simple interest, computed from November 28, 2026 until the balance is paid in full. If the parties intend this to be an interest-free loan, the rate stated above is 0% per year. The Interest-Rate Limit clause of this document describes the ceiling California law places on whatever rate is stated, depending on whether this loan is used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes or for some other purpose.

REPAYMENT
Jordan Lee will repay this Note as follows: Repaid in 12 equal monthly installments of $433.34, beginning January 1, 2027. Regardless of that schedule, the entire unpaid principal balance, together with all accrued and unpaid interest, is due and payable in full no later than December 1, 2027 (the "Maturity Date"). Payment is made by: _______________________________________________.

DEFAULT
Jordan Lee is in default under this Note if a payment required by the repayment schedule above is not made within _______ days of its due date, or if the entire remaining balance is not paid by the Maturity Date. On default, the entire unpaid principal balance and all accrued, unpaid interest become due and payable in full immediately, at Pat Morgan's election, without further notice or demand, unless Pat Morgan agrees in writing to waive or extend that right for a particular missed payment. Because this Note is unsecured, a default does not by itself give Pat Morgan a right to take or sell any specific property of Jordan Lee to satisfy the debt; collecting on this Note after a default, whether informally or through a lawsuit, is subject to the general rules on suing to collect a debt, including the time limit on bringing suit described in the Time Limit to Sue on This Note clause of this document.

TIME LIMIT TO SUE ON THIS NOTE
A lawsuit Pat Morgan brings to collect on this Note is subject to California's statute of limitations for an action founded on a written instrument. Code of Civil Procedure section 337 sets that period at four years for an action upon any contract, obligation, or liability founded upon an instrument in writing — a category a signed written promissory note falls within — subject to an exception, in Code of Civil Procedure section 336a, that does not concern an ordinary unsecured promissory note between individuals like Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee. Code of Civil Procedure section 312 states the more general rule underlying this limit: a civil action can only be commenced within the period a statute such as section 337 prescribes, counted from when the cause of action accrues. Once the applicable four-year period has run, a court action to collect the unpaid balance of this Note is ordinarily time-barred.

[This clause's source hasn't been independently confirmed against the government's own primary text yet (it's sourced to a secondary copy, or hasn't been checked at all). Treat the quote below as a starting point, not a confirmed fact, until it is.]
  "An action upon any contract, obligation or liability founded upon an instrument in writing, except as provided in Section 336a of this code"
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 337 (law.onecle.com text), California Code of Civil Procedure, four-year period for an action on a written instrument (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil-procedure/337.html)
  "Civil actions, without exception, can only be commenced within the periods prescribed in this title, after the cause of action shall have accrued, unless where, in special cases, a different limitation is prescribed by statute."
  — Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 312 (law.onecle.com text), California Code of Civil Procedure, civil actions may only be commenced within the prescribed period after accrual (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil-procedure/312.html)

NO WITNESS OR NOTARIZATION REQUIRED BY STATUTE
California statute does not require a promissory note between private individuals to be witnessed or notarized (acknowledged before a notary public) for it to be an enforceable contract. Civil Code section 1550 lists what state law treats as essential to the existence of a contract: parties capable of contracting, their consent, a lawful object, and a sufficient cause or consideration.   "It is essential to the existence of a contract that there should be: 1. Parties capable of contracting; 2. Their consent; 3. A lawful object; and, 4. A sufficient cause or consideration."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1550 (law.onecle.com text), California Civil Code, the four elements essential to the existence of a contract (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil/1550.html)
  "“negotiable instrument” means an unconditional promise or order to pay a fixed amount of money, with or without interest or other charges described in the promise or order, if it is all of the following"
  — Cal. Com. Code § 3104(a) (law.onecle.com text), California Commercial Code, definition of a negotiable instrument / note (https://law.onecle.com/california/commercial/3104.html)

Signed:

Borrower: _______________________ Date: _______________
Printed name: Jordan Lee

Lender: _______________________ Date: _______________
Printed name: Pat Morgan
